addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It contains near term tasks with a
short description and uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][M] (done)
- [[N]] [<title>][M] (current)
- [[N]] [<title>][M]
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][M]

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<one `#####` subsection per rung, closing included, headed by its exact title, opened at
laddering with the rung's intent and completed at landing with the conceptual delta, the
closing rung's at close-out with gotchas in problem/solution form>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

### feat: measure reproducibility

#### Problem

Modern CPUs change their clock frequency continuously to save power. The OS's **power policy**
(the cpufreq governor plus, on AMD, the EPP hint) decides how eagerly the chip boosts under load
and how quickly it retreats, so the clock a run executes at depends on the box's recent history,
not its spec sheet. A latency number is cycles times cycle time, and the 2026-08-03 experiment
showed both failure shapes: under `powersave` the same code differed ~9% run to run as the clock
wandered, and a run parked on the un-boosted base clock graded A, flat being all the grade sees.
For A/B comparison the need is consistency, not speed: a stable clock at any rate beats an
unstable fast one. Today the harness cannot report the policy, cannot hold the clock still, and
no run's numbers survive the session that produced them, so a reader cannot tell a code delta
from a power-management delta. (Continues the cycle stalled since 2026-08-04.)

1	# custom-family.md - iiac-perf's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family
2	
3	Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
4	member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
5	one.
6	
7	**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
8	here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
9	<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
10	converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
11	that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.
12	
13	## Medium and validation
14	
15	The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
16	`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).
17	
18	**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
19	a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
20	readers of the history (see
21	[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
22	contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.
23	
24	- **Full validation**
25	  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
26	  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
27	    1. `cargo fmt`
28	    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
29	    3. `cargo test`
30	    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
31	    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
32	- **Fast validation**
33	  - when: ladder checklist step 3
34	  - `cargo test --bins`
35	
36	The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
37	universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).
38	
39	## Membership
40	
41	- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
42	- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`
43	
44	These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
45	`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
46	rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
47	fail its own validator.
48	
49	## Messaging
50	
51	Members notify each other through the `../vc-x1-messages` repo, one file per recipient, ours being
52	`../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`. The protocol is that repo's `README.md` and it governs. Message
53	bodies live in the sender's own repo (ours under `messages/`), and the messages repo holds only
54	pointer records. It replaced the template repository's mailboxes 2026-08-13, with the design
55	record in [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo). These are
56	the parts that decide how a session behaves.
57	
58	- **At acquaint, read `../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`.** Records sit newest first. A record with
59	  no `read` field is unread mail, and one with no `outcome-*` field is still open.
60	- **Mark, never delete.** Our file's persistence policy keeps every record: reading one adds a
61	  `read:` timestamp, and handling one adds `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` pointing at what
62	  came of it, usually a `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` section. The outcome closes the record, and
63	  the `read:` is what tells the sender it arrived.
64	- **Records are thin pointers, not state.** A record carries `local:` / `remote:` references to
65	  the body, so anything worth keeping is already a committed file in the sender's repo, and the
66	  old copy-before-delete step (learned 2026-08-05) is obsolete.
67	- **Whoever writes a record commits it**, in the messages repo. Write to a member's file there,
68	  never into their repo: a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent.
69	- **Durable mail is push-then-record.** A `remote:` field is a commit permalink, so the body's
70	  commit pushes before the record naming it is written. Local-only records are fine for same-day
71	  traffic between siblings.
72	
73	## Dogfood log
74	
75	Dated entries on what this project is trying and where the pinned instructions chafed, failed, or
76	got amended: the evidence base for the family's convergence decisions
77	([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
78	
79	Each entry carries a **status**: `proposed` (in our agent-files, awaiting the family),
80	`adopted family-wide`, `rejected`, or `permanently local`. In-flight entries only: on
81	resolution an entry retires to [done.md](notes/done.md) with its narrative in
82	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, adopted and rejected alike. Entries predating the status
83	convention keep their form until touched.
84	
85	- 2026-08-14 (`proposed`): the semicolon allowance goes, and the agent-files sweep to zero
86	  - the pinned rule blessed the "between equals" join and left everything else a judgment call.
87	    wink's observation: agents take advantage of the exceptions, so the allowance is claimed
88	    wherever a semicolon is wanted
89	  - the rule is now flat: prose carries no semicolons, and a semicolon appears only in code
90	    (code spans, fenced code, source files), where it is syntax. Each prose site converts to a
91	    period, a comma with a conjunction, or sub-bullets
92	  - the agent-files (custom* included) carry no historical exemption and sweep to zero. Any
93	    other historical file keeps its semicolons only until altered, and altering one means
94	    asking the user whether they should go (wink, tightened mid-rung from a silent
95	    convert-when-touched). Excluding src/'s ~125 existing comment-line joins from this cycle's
96	    sweep is wink's call, keeping it focused on agent-file convergence
97	  - the rule tightened is one vc-x1 wrote and swept at ~140 sites. Proposed to them by message
98	    after this cycle lands, with their own instruction back: review the rule, not each instance
99	  - rationale in
100	    [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-semicolons-leave-the-agent-files)
101	
102	- 2026-08-12 (`proposed`): validation runs at every commit, and the notes-only skip goes
103	  - the per-commit checklist stamped the version-of-record at step 4 and let step 5 be skipped
104	    for notes-only commits, so a commit could carry a version that no build ever had. Measured
105	    the same day: 0.24.5 and 0.24.6 both stamped and neither built, and `-V` answered 0.24.4
106	    until the next close-out jumped it three
107	  - wink's rule and his reason: every commit bumps the version precisely so a build exists
108	    carrying it, which makes an unbuilt bump a version nobody can run and the banner a claim
109	    nobody checked
110	  - so the skip goes at all three sites, and the step is conditioned on the medium rather than on
111	    the commit: run the artifact if the medium has one to run (wink). A first draft made the
112	    escape "too costly to build", which asks every project to judge its own cost and would be
113	    claimed by anyone who found validation tedious
114	  - each of the three sites gets one job so the rule is written once (wink): the checklist
115	    instructs, the protocol holds the reason and the medium condition, and `custom.md` holds the
116	    commands. A first pass had the checklist and the protocol carrying the same sentence
117	  - the same pass fixed a step number this morning's sync left stale, and dropped a
118	    cycle-at-a-glance clause that named validation as a close-out specialty. The stale number is
119	    the argument in miniature: it was a restatement, which is what let it drift unnoticed
120	  - rationale in [chores-06](notes/chores/chores-06.md#docs-validate-every-commit)
121	
122	- 2026-08-07 (`proposed`): the family layer splits out of `custom.md`
123	  - `custom.md` had been accumulating things that only make sense because this repo belongs to a
124	    family: a member name, a template path, and a dogfood log whose status vocabulary reads
125	    `adopted family-wide`. wink's test is that `custom.md` should be usable as-is by a project that
126	    has never heard of us, and it failed that test
127	  - so the family layer moves here, and `custom.md` shrinks to a stub with nothing to substitute:
128	    a title naming no project, and one section. A member's copy differs from the payload's by the
129	    single conventions entry that points here, so `diff custom.md <template>/work/custom.md` is one
130	    line for every member
131	  - the pointer is that entry rather than an intro sentence (wink). We argued for the intro, on the
132	    grounds that four members carrying an identical one-line diff looks like a fake divergence.
133	    The answer is that it is a real project convention, and one line is cheaper than a paragraph
134	    every member has to keep in sync
135	  - the chain is `AGENTS.md` -> `custom.md` -> here, all of it prose, which is what lets the pinned
136	    set stay ignorant of the split. A non-member has no entry and no file
137	  - `CLAUDE.md` collapses to one line, `@AGENTS.md` (wink). It had grown a second `@` import per
138	    layer, which made it a second statement of what to read and therefore a second thing to keep
139	    true. Now `AGENTS.md` is the only source of that truth, and `CLAUDE.md` is payload-identical for
140	    every project, member or not. The cost is real and worth stating: nothing below `AGENTS.md` is
141	    auto-loaded any more, so hard rule 0 is load-bearing rather than a formality
142	  - one consequence needs the family's agreement, not ours: **"Check the mailbox at acquaint" leaves
143	    the pinned `AGENTS.md`** and lands in `## Messaging` above. vc-x1 pinned it in the 20260802
144	    snapshot, so this is a reversal. The argument is that a non-member cannot perform it at all,
145	    since building the mailbox path needs a member name and a template path they do not have, so it
146	    is dead text naming concepts they lack rather than a harmless no-op
147	  - deliberately not opened in the same pass: `AGENTS.md` still says "the family" and "member" where
148	    the generic mechanism is "the template payload and my copy of it". Same inconsistency one level
149	    up, and folding it in would roughly double the review surface of an already large configuration
150

# custom-family.md - iiac-perf's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family

Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).

## Membership

- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
fail its own validator.

## Messaging

Members notify each other through the `../vc-x1-messages` repo, one file per recipient, ours being
`../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`. The protocol is that repo's `README.md` and it governs. Message
bodies live in the sender's own repo (ours under `messages/`), and the messages repo holds only
pointer records. It replaced the template repository's mailboxes 2026-08-13, with the design
record in [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo). These are
the parts that decide how a session behaves.

- **At acquaint, read `../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`.** Records sit newest first. A record with
  no `read` field is unread mail, and one with no `outcome-*` field is still open.
- **Mark, never delete.** Our file's persistence policy keeps every record: reading one adds a
  `read:` timestamp, and handling one adds `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` pointing at what
  came of it, usually a `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` section. The outcome closes the record, and
  the `read:` is what tells the sender it arrived.
- **Records are thin pointers, not state.** A record carries `local:` / `remote:` references to
  the body, so anything worth keeping is already a committed file in the sender's repo, and the
  old copy-before-delete step (learned 2026-08-05) is obsolete.
- **Whoever writes a record commits it**, in the messages repo. Write to a member's file there,
  never into their repo: a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent.
- **Durable mail is push-then-record.** A `remote:` field is a commit permalink, so the body's
  commit pushes before the record naming it is written. Local-only records are fine for same-day
  traffic between siblings.

## Dogfood log

Dated entries on what this project is trying and where the pinned instructions chafed, failed, or
got amended: the evidence base for the family's convergence decisions
([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).

`adopted family-wide`, `rejected`, or `permanently local`. In-flight entries only: on
resolution an entry retires to [done.md](notes/done.md) with its narrative in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, adopted and rejected alike. Entries predating the status
convention keep their form until touched.

  - the pinned rule blessed the "between equals" join and left everything else a judgment call.
    wink's observation: agents take advantage of the exceptions, so the allowance is claimed
    wherever a semicolon is wanted
  - the rule is now flat: prose carries no semicolons, and a semicolon appears only in code
    (code spans, fenced code, source files), where it is syntax. Each prose site converts to a
    period, a comma with a conjunction, or sub-bullets
  - the agent-files (custom* included) carry no historical exemption and sweep to zero. Any
    other historical file keeps its semicolons only until altered, and altering one means
    asking the user whether they should go (wink, tightened mid-rung from a silent
    convert-when-touched). Excluding src/'s ~125 existing comment-line joins from this cycle's
    sweep is wink's call, keeping it focused on agent-file convergence

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

The version above is the record format's, and changes to it are additive. A field is added, never
renamed or repurposed, so a reader written against an older version still reads today's records.
A major bump would mean that stopped being true and there has not been one.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
nothing.

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z iiac-perf

- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/messages/test-msg.md#message1

The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.

Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
section slug.

- `local:` the message's local file reference.
- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.

  unread. Receipt is not completion: a record stays open until it carries an outcome, so a
  member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `outcome-*` field, and `read` is
  what tells the sender their message arrived.
- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
  both halves of an exchange, and their arrival is what closes a record.

A handled record, this one sent the other way, as it would sit in `iiac-perf.md`. Two things are
worth noticing. The body is vc-x1's specimen under `notes/messages/` where iiac-perf's sits
under `messages/`, because a body lives wherever its sender chooses. And the `remote:` was
written only after the body's commit pushed, the ordering rule from
[Two modes](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) obeyed in this very example, since a permalink cannot
precede the commit it names. The exchange is staged but every reference is live:

a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read. A record carries no version of its own, since its
commit dates it against this file's history.

**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.

## Two modes, fast and durable

The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.

- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
  that push made resolvable.

**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.

**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
push.

## Whoever writes a record commits it

Whoever writes a record is the one who commits it. In the same act is the ideal, since then no
moment holds an uncommitted record, but with today's handful of friendly participants a short
delay or batching a few writes into one commit is fine. What does not relax is the ownership:
nobody commits someone else's writing, which is what this repo has instead of a manager, because
ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## Concurrent writes collide, and the collision is normal

Every new record goes directly below its file's header, so two writers active at the same time
conflict at exactly the same lines. The merge is trivial, keep both records in either order, and
it is the expected cost of newest-first rather than an error. No record depends on its
neighbours, which is what makes the resolution safe.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. Settled as a
  rule at vc-x1's review (2026-08-13): the one real risk, a sender imposing a policy, is already
  defused by the no-policy-at-birth clause.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

**On the redundancy, you're half right, and it's the important half:**

The paragraph is a demonstrable editing accident (an orphaned tail from a replaced paragraph), the redundant sentence violates the family's own one-statement-per-rule instinct, and the depth note's content belongs beside the depth transform it qualifies. Its first sentence repeats what Chores sections already says, but its second sentence (the heading-depth note) is genuinely unique and worth keeping. I suggest we skip copying it as-is and instead propose the fix: delete the redundant sentence and relocate the depth note into the Chores sections transform list, then tell vc-x1. I think the template-branch route is right, and it fixes a cost our own dogfood log already recorded. A few thoughts to sharpen it:

**Why it's better than diff-only.** The documented mechanism ("the diff between a member and the payload is the member's open proposal set") has a known weakness we wrote down on 2026-08-07: nothing at acquaint shows a reader which parts of a member's pinned copy are family-agreed, and reading the diff is manual. Your transience worry is the same weakness from the other side: as this repo keeps moving, a one-paragraph proposal is easy to lose in the noise, and vc-x1 has to fish it out of our history. A branch on the template gives the proposal a neutral, stable home, makes review a one-command diff against template `main`, and makes acceptance mechanical: you land the branch, both members re-sync, the diff empties. It uses the template as exactly the coordination point it's declared to be.

**It's a mechanism trial, so let's say so.** This is a new convergence move the agent-files don't describe. I'd give it a dogfood-log entry (`proposed`: "convergence proposals ride template branches"), so if it works it can become the family's convention and if it chafes we have the record. That also preempts the objection that "the payload is never edited": a branch isn't the payload, `main` is, but the message to vc-x1 should be explicit that template `main` remains untouched and the branch is offer, not baseline.

**Who commits on the template.** The heads-up says the template stays agent-less with wink as operator. Me committing a proposal branch there under your explicit direction seems within the spirit (agent-less means no session of its own, not no writes), but the commit and the message should both say it was done at your direction, so vc-x1 doesn't read it as an agent unilaterally writing the coordination repo.

**Two copies during review.** Once the change lives both here and on the branch, revisions during review have to touch both. For one paragraph that's cheap, but worth deciding up front: the branch is the authoritative proposal text, and our local copy re-syncs to whatever lands.

**Sequencing details on our side:**

- Convention work runs as its own cycle, never a rung in the feature ladder, so this is a small dedicated docs cycle interleaved into the stalled `measure reproducibility` gap (precedent: the messaging fix at 0.25.3), on its own topic bookmark per rule 13.
- The message should be durable mode (the body's commit pushed before the record is written), and should name our base explicitly (template `main` at d6aaaaf1 / their 181e760d), since vc-x1 is mid-restructure on the 0816-proposal and `cycle-protocol.md` is a file they could plausibly touch. Naming the base makes any race visible instead of confusing.
- The proposal text itself: delete the redundant first sentence, fold the depth note into the first transform bullet in `## Chores sections` (the one already covering depth under a program heading), reworded to fit the bullet. The branch and our copy carry identical final text.

One small counterpoint to have considered: the pure diff-is-proposal route is one fewer artifact and is the documented mechanism, so we're adding process. I think the addition pays for itself here precisely because our repo is busy, but if vc-x1 pushes back that branches recreate the "maintained proposal artifacts" problem the diff design was built to kill, that's a fair debate for the convergence review, and the dogfood entry is where our reasoning waits for it.

The plain version: I agree with your plan. Edit here, mirror it as a branch on the template committed at your direction, message vc-x1 with a pointer to the branch and our reasoning, and log the "proposals ride template branches" idea as its own proposed convention. Run it as a small standalone docs cycle, not part of the current feature cycle. No action taken yet.

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional). A
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties. So a
19	single-step cycle is one commit, and a multi-step is minimum two (a Work commit plus the
20	close-out), typically three or more (the definition is
21	[AGENTS.md's Terminology](../AGENTS.md#terminology)). The
22	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
23	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
24	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
25	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
26	
27	## Cycles run on a bookmark
28	
29	A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work repo, created at the opening and named by the
30	cycle title's slug (the anchor algorithm in
31	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). `main` advances only when the
32	finished cycle lands on it, and nothing pushes straight to `main`. The bot repo needs no bookmark:
33	its `main` rides the tip of its linear narrative.
34	
35	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
36	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
37	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
38	  that makes the cycle permanent.
39	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
40	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
41	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
42	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
43	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
44	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
45	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
46	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
47	
48	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
49	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
50	
51	## Opening checklist
52	
53	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
54	
55	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
56	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
57	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
58	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
59	   title, `####` items, and under a program heading, each one deeper):
60	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
61	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
62	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
63	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
64	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
65	     `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References`. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`,
66	     is linked like the rest
67	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
68	     deliberate)
69	   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, closing included, headed
70	   by the rung's exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs
71	   land, the closing rung's at close-out (see the protocol's
72	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
73	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
74	   version-of-record.
75	
76	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
77	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
78	
79	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
80	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
81	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
82	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
83	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
84	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
85	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
86	
87	## Committing vs pushing
88	
89	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
90	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
91	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
92	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
93	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
94	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
95	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
96	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
97	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
98	
99	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
100	
101	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
102	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
103	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
104	
105	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
106	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
107	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
108	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
109	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**:
110	  - the bookmark has already landed
111	  - another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase
112	  - the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees
113	
114	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
115	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
116	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
117	
118	## Per-commit checklist
119	
120	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
121	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
122	
123	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
124	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
125	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
126	   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
127	   rung was laddered, and the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
128	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
129	4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
130	   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
131	   commit.
132	5. Validate the artifact at every commit, doc-only ones included. The medium's commands are in
133	   [custom.md](../custom.md).
134	6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
135	   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
136	   review is likely complete.
137	7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a body in
138	   prose.md's [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form) (an intro paragraph stating the
139	   general problem, `*` bullets for its facets, `-` bullets for solutions, a `-` solving the
140	   nearest enclosing problem), sized per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in
141	   either, no file list (the diff is the mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo,
142	   and the session hold that). See [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
143	8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
144	   explicitly includes it.
145	9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
146	   `jj commit`. Never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
147	
148	## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist
149	
150	Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
151	[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):
152	
153	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
154	2. Do the commit's work.
155	3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
156	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
157	   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.
158	
159	Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
160	(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
161	publishes the single commit.
162	
163	## Before any push
164	
165	- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
166	  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
167	  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
168	  bounded task only. Delegation waives stops, never flow (records, validation, the bookmark
169	  discipline, per the protocol's [Policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy)), and destructive ops
170	  still pause.
171	- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
172	- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).
173	
174	## After the final push: hard stop
175	
176	Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
177	verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
178	words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
179	after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
180	or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
181	delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps. The hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
182	push. See
183	[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).
184	
185	## Close-out checklist
186	
187	The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
188	[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):
189	
190	1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
191	   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
192	   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
193	2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
194	   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
195	   markers, add any design subsections, and complete the closing rung's subsection: gotchas in
196	   problem/solution form, `_None._` when closing surfaced none.
197	3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.
198	   Four transforms, two of which fail silently: headings one level deeper, rung refs renumbered
199	   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes
200	   rewritten. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). Add the title-only
201	   `## Table of Contents` entry.
202	4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,
203	   detail as sub-bullets (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Replace the
204	   `## In Progress` block with `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
205	5. Full validation, mandatory.
206	6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
207	7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
208	   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
209	   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is
210	   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
211	8. **Land the bookmark** on the user's go. Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent.
212	   Once `main` contains the bookmark, delete it, locally and remotely. See
213	   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
214	9. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for the
215	   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's
216	   share. Never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch. The backfill edits ride the next
217	   push (a commit cannot record its own SHA).
218	
219	## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind
220	
221	Three, independent of project language:
222	
223	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
224	  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
225	  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
226	  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
227	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
228	  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
229	  reports. Getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
230	  tool infers.
231	- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
232	  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
     deliberate)
   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, closing included, headed
   by the rung's exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs
   land, the closing rung's at close-out (see the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
   version-of-record.

Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**:
  - the bookmark has already landed
  - another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase
  - the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
   rung was laddered, and the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
   commit.
5. Validate the artifact at every commit, doc-only ones included. The medium's commands are in
   [custom.md](../custom.md).
6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
   review is likely complete.
7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a body in
   prose.md's [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form) (an intro paragraph stating the
   general problem, `*` bullets for its facets, `-` bullets for solutions, a `-` solving the
   nearest enclosing problem), sized per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in
   either, no file list (the diff is the mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo,
   and the session hold that). See [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`. Never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only. Delegation waives stops, never flow (records, validation, the bookmark
  discipline, per the protocol's [Policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy)), and destructive ops
  still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps. The hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
   markers, add any design subsections, and complete the closing rung's subsection: gotchas in
   problem/solution form, `_None._` when closing surfaced none.
3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.
   Four transforms, two of which fail silently: headings one level deeper, rung refs renumbered
   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes
   rewritten. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). Add the title-only
   `## Table of Contents` entry.
4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,
   detail as sub-bullets (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Replace the
   `## In Progress` block with `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
5. Full validation, mandatory.
6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
8. **Land the bookmark** on the user's go. Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent.
   Once `main` contains the bookmark, delete it, locally and remotely. See
   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
9. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for the
   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's
   share. Never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch. The backfill edits ride the next
   push (a commit cannot record its own SHA).

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports. Getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
4	suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
5	copied **verbatim**, with
6	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
7	conditional rather than per-project edits.
8	
9	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
10	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
11	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
12	
13	## Terms
14	
15	Three names, used as defined here across
16	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
17	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
18	
19	- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
20	  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
21	  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
22	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
23	  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
24	  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
25	- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
26	  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
27	  artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## A stamp, not a name
31	
32	The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
33	named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
34	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
35	suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
36	inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.
37	
38	## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides
39	
40	Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
41	touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**
42	
43	- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
44	  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
45	  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
46	  presentation, docs, notes.
47	- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
48	  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
49	- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
50	  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).
51	
52	**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
53	thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.
54	
55	## Grammar and storage
56	
57	One spelling everywhere the version is written:
58	
59	```
60	<public>[-<suffix>]
61	```
62	
63	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
64	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
65	  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
66	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
67	  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
68	  version storable in every medium below.
69	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
70	  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability, while manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a
71	  leading `v`. Cargo rejects one.)
72	
73	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
74	
75	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
76	  valid at any dot depth.
77	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
78	  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
79	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
80	  adds its case to
81	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
82	
83	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
84	
85	- **The stored version identifies but does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
86	  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out), while PEP 440 sorts the
87	  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
88	  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
89	  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
90	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
91	  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
92	  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.
93	
94	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
95	multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
96	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
97	`+` are all invalid. `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth. `1.2.3-1` parses but
98	silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
99	every medium accepts.
100	
101	## Recording the version-of-record
102	
103	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
104	the case that fits your medium:
105	
106	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
107	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
108	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
109	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
110	    ...). Add the case as needed
111	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
112	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
113	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
114	    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
115	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
116	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
117	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
118	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
119	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
120	  per-commit preference.
121	
122	## Dev artifact name
123	
124	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
125	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
126	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
127	
128	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
129	  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
130	  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
131	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
132	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
133	  install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
135	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
136	  flow's install.
137	
138	Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
139	its `custom.md` layer.
140	
141	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
142	
143	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
144	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
145	
146	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
147	  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
148	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
149	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
150	  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
151	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
152	
153	## Suffix scheme
154	
155	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
156	each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157	
158	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159	not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160	neither a number nor a version (see
161	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162	prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163	commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164	nothing dereferences one.
165	
166	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
168	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169	
170	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
171	and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
172	Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
173	without renumbering siblings.
174	
175	Disambiguation:
176	
177	- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
178	- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
179	
180	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
181	
182	- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
183	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
184	- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
185	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
186	
187	Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
188	step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
189	above, every commit carries a distinct version.
