every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
14	or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
15	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
16	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
17	fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
18	they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
19	naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
20	[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
21	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
28	  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
32	  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
33	  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
34	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).
35	
36	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
37	
38	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged
39	  by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
40	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
41	    meets first and it answers the problem
42	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
43	    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
44	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
45	    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
46	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
47	    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
48	    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
49	    here
50	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
51	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
52	  list. See
53	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
54	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
55	
56	### Line widths
57	
58	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
59	than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
60	2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
61	
62	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
63	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
64	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
65	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
66	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
67	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
68	
69	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
70	when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
71	imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
72	a literal report row, indented code in a comment).
73	
74	### Problem-first shape
75	
76	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
77	form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
78	
79	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
80	  what follows it.
81	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
82	  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
83	  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
84	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
85	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
86	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
87	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
88	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
89	    picked up into a cycle.
90	
91	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
92	cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
93	commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
94	commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
95	here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
96	unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.
97	
98	### Commit-body form
99	
100	A commit body is the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
101	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
102	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a
103	solution statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and
104	separately.
105	
106	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It
107	  is mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is
108	  a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
109	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
110	  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
111	  usually asking to be more than one commit.
112	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
113	  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
114	  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
115	- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
116	  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.
117	
118	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
119	Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
120	solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
121	every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
122	terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
123	carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
124	is wrong to normalize them.
125	
126	Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
127	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
128	
129	### Semicolons
130	
131	Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
132	files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is
133	written explicitly instead:
134	
135	- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
136	  history keeps the record.").
137	- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
138	  onward rather than making its own claim.
139	- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so
140	  the structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather
141	  than separating with semicolons.
142	
143	The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code
144	first, then expects zero.
145	
146	The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are
147	swept to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is altered:
148	altering one is the moment to ask the user whether its semicolons should be removed, always,
149	never a license to convert or keep them silently.
150	
151	### Typeable punctuation only
152	
153	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
154	*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
155	below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
156	Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
157	paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
158	Like the semicolon rule above this one is absolute, and stricter with history: no ask-on-alter,
159	no exemption at all, because a banned character costs nothing to write and is paid on every
160	read, so a soft rule accumulates them.
161	
162	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
163	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
164	
165	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
166	  sub-bullets.
167	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
168	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
169	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
170	  go.
171	
172	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
173	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
174	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
175	commit.
176	
177	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
178	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
179	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
180	prose. It applies going forward, and existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
181	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
182	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
183	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
184	
185	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
186	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
187	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
188	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
189	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
190	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
191	
192	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
193	
194	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
195	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
196	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
197	They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the
198	[Commit-body form](#commit-body-form), ladder / chores are conceptual (see "Bullet *content*
199	differs by surface" above). The shared template:
200	
201	```
202	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
203	<optional prose intro>
204	  - <optional item>
205	    <optional prose intro>
206	      - <optional sub-item>
207	      ...
208	```
209	
210	The three surfaces apply it as:
211	
212	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is
213	  `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)`: the as-built `[[N]]` placeholder carried from birth, the
214	  title reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's
215	  `# References` (the closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
216	  Its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its
217	  text says so. Detail lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection
218	  headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
219	  [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
220	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
221	  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
222	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
223	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
224	  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).
225	
226	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
227	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection
228	heading carries the same title, a fourth surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only
229	when close-out gotchas occurred: see the protocol's
230	[Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
231	
232	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
233	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
234	section header carries the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the
235	bookends below). To keep a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
236	step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
237	
238	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a
239	suffix, " opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
240	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
241	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the chores `##` header and
242	the `## Done` entry carry it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the
243	closing rung's subsection anchor clear of the section header's. A single-step cycle's one
244	commit is the cycle and keeps the bare title. The type repeats across the pair even though the
245	bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make them scannable. Rungs between keep
246	their own titles on the stem.
247	
248	### Steps are named, not numbered
249	
250	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
251	entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
252	the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.
253	
254	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
255	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
256	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
257	  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
258	  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
259	  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
260	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
261	  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
262	  come along. See
263	  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
264	- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
265	  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
266	  and are equally never used as references.
267	
268	### Versions live in the version-of-record only
269	
270	No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
271	title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
272	[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
273	commit.
274	
275	**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
276	for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
277	one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
278	residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.
279	
280	**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
281	which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:
282	
283	- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
284	  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
285	  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
286	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
287	- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
288	  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
289	  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
290	  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.
291	
292	The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
293	because a commit cannot record its own SHA. A Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
294	is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
295	unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
296	([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
297	published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.
298	
299	**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
300	opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
301	scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
302	rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
303	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
304	one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.
305	
306	## Pinned files name no project
307	
308	A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
309	history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
310	shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.
311	
312	**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
313	history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
314	different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
315	records, while the rule outlives it.
316	
317	**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file, and leave the evidence trail
318	in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
319	that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
320	specimen in
321	the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
322	reference, per the same distinction
323	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
324	draws.
325	
326	## Speculation marker
327	
328	Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
329	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
330	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
331	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
332	
333	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
334	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
335	worth keeping visible in the written record.
336	
337	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
338	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
339	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
340	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
341	on hand.
342	
343	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
344	
345	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
346	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
347	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
348	
349	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread, and the plain form catches
350	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
351	
352	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
353	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
354	synopsis.

# Prose and durable text

How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
comments, chores sections).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged
  by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
    meets first and it answers the problem
  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
    here
- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
  list. See
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
a literal report row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
  what follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
    picked up into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.

### Commit-body form

A commit body is the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a
solution statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and
separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It
  is mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is
  a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
  usually asking to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).

### Semicolons

Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is
written explicitly instead:

- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
  history keeps the record.").
- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
  onward rather than making its own claim.
- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so
  the structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather
  than separating with semicolons.

The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code
first, then expects zero.

The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are
swept to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is altered:
altering one is the moment to ask the user whether its semicolons should be removed, always,
never a license to convert or keep them silently.

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
Like the semicolon rule above this one is absolute, and stricter with history: no ask-on-alter,
no exemption at all, because a banned character costs nothing to write and is paid on every
read, so a soft rule accumulates them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
  sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
  go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward, and existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the
[Commit-body form](#commit-body-form), ladder / chores are conceptual (see "Bullet *content*
differs by surface" above). The shared template:

```
<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is
  `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)`: the as-built `[[N]]` placeholder carried from birth, the
  title reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's
  `# References` (the closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
  Its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its
  text says so. Detail lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection
  headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
  [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection
heading carries the same title, a fourth surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only
when close-out gotchas occurred: see the protocol's
[Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the
bookends below). To keep a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a
suffix, " opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the chores `##` header and
the `## Done` entry carry it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the
closing rung's subsection anchor clear of the section header's. A single-step cycle's one
commit is the cycle and keeps the bare title. The type repeats across the pair even though the
bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make them scannable. Rungs between keep
their own titles on the stem.

### Steps are named, not numbered

A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.

- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
  come along. See
  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
  and are equally never used as references.

### Versions live in the version-of-record only

No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
commit.

**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.

**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:

- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.

The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
because a commit cannot record its own SHA. A Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.

**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.

## Pinned files name no project

A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.

**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
records, while the rule outlives it.

**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file, and leave the evidence trail
in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
specimen in
the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
reference, per the same distinction
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
draws.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread, and the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## File reads: read the slice you need
13	
14	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
15	further on demand.
16	
17	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
18	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
19	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
20	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
21	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
22	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
23	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
24	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
25	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
26	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
27	  need.
28	
29	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
30	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
31	to historical files.
32	
33	## Notes references
34	
35	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
36	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
37	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
38	single-bracketed.
39	
40	## Reference numbering
41	
42	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
43	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
44	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
45	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
46	
47	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
48	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
49	file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
50	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
51	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
52	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
53	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
54	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
55	
56	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
57	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
58	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
59	as-built ladder, or a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own
60	subsection. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
61	exact shape.
62	
63	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
64	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md` is `## Todo`
65	then `## Done`, `chores-NN.md` top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
66	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
67	definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
68	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
69	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule. `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
70	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate, while `chores-NN.md` / `done.md`
71	are append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
72	slots out of document order).
73	
74	## Markdown anchor links
75	
76	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
77	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
78	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
79	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
80	official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
81	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
82	
83	## Todo format
84	
85	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest, with
86	the long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
87	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
88	description with reference links to more detail.
89	
90	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
91	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending), and for `## Bugs` it's
92	just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
93	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
94	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
95	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
96	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
97	
98	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
99	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
100	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
101	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
102	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
103	
104	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
105	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
106	
107	Example shape:
108	
109	```
110	# Todo
111	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
112	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
113	
114	# Done
115	- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]
116	
117	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
118	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
119	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
120	```
121	
122	## Done entry form
123	
124	A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
125	title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:
126	
127	```
128	- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
129	  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
130	  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
131	```
132	
133	- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
134	  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
135	  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
136	  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
137	  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
138	- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
139	  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
140	  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
141	  line, trades one of those for the other. See
142	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
143	  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
144	- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
145	  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
146	- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
147	  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
148	- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
149	  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.
150	
151	## Retiring Done entries
152	
153	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
154	log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:
155	
156	- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
157	  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
158	  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
159	- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
160	  version-of-record.
161	- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
162	  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
163	  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
164	  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
165	  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).
166	
167	Migration mechanics:
168	
169	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
170	  number).
171	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
172	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
173	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
174	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
175	
176	## Chores conventions
177	
178	### Headings and entries that record a commit
179	
180	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
181	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
182	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
183	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
184	version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
185	are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
186	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
187	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
188	`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
189	(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
190	[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
191	[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).
192	
193	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
194	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
195	whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
196	commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
197	match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
198	record up with its commit.
199	
200	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
201	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
202	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
203	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
204	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
205	
206	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
207	free-form text. The convention applies going forward.
208	
209	### Chores section content: no edit list, git is the record
210	
211	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
212	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
213	design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
214	rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
215	**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
216	changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
217	body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
218	source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others, and none
219	restates another.
220	
221	The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
222	`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
223	narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
224	than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
225	[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
226	two don't drift.
227	
228	**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
229	chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
230	drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.
231	
232	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
233	Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
234	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
235	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
236	direction).
237	
238	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
239	places, and detail written twice drifts. The division:
240	
241	- git owns the mechanical record
242	- the body owns the problem and the solution
243	- chores owns the narrative
244	- the ladder's commit refs link them
245	
246	### Chores commit references
247	
248	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
249	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
250	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
251	one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:
252	
253	```
254	## refactor: extract config loader
255	
256	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
257	- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader
258	
259	<intro paragraph...>
260	```
261	
262	- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
263	  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
264	  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment (`[M]: #<slug>`): it
265	  rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the subsections move into the same
266	  file, renumbered like any other slot, the closing rung's among them. No step number and no
267	  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
268	  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
269	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
270	- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
271	  (see
272	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
273	  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
274	  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
275	  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
276	  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
277	  falsify.
278	- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
279	  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
280	  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
281	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
282	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
283	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
284	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
285	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`. The inner `[3]`
286	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
287	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
288	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
289	
290	```
291	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
292	```
293	
294	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
295	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
296	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
297	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
298	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
299	
300	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
301	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
302	is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
303	opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
304	the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
305	lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
306	cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
307	
308	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
309	going forward.
310	
311	### Chores file Table of Contents
312	
313	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
314	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
315	section, in file order.
316	
317	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
318	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
319	- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
320	  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
321	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
322	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
323
