# Notes file conventions

Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
before editing a notes file.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## File reads: read the slice you need

Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
further on demand.

- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
  need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
to historical files.

## Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
single-bracketed.

## Reference numbering

Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.

A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
as-built ladder, or a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own
subsection. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
exact shape.

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md` is `## Todo`
then `## Done`, `chores-NN.md` top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule. `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate, while `chores-NN.md` / `done.md`
are append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
slots out of document order).

## Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

## Todo format

`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest, with
the long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
description with reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending), and for `## Bugs` it's
just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Done entry form

A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:

```
- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
```

- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
  line, trades one of those for the other. See
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.
- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text. The convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list, git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others, and none
restates another.

The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
two don't drift.

**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. The division:

- git owns the mechanical record
- the body owns the problem and the solution
- chores owns the narrative
- the ladder's commit refs link them

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment (`[M]: #<slug>`): it
  rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the subsections move into the same
  file, renumbered like any other slot, the closing rung's among them. No step number and no
  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
  falsify.
- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`. The inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never rebased"
wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Resolvability

A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves to the same chid in every
clone. Cloning the bot repo gave the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone.
We think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it survives `jj git clone` /
fetch.

The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh random chid for `@` in each
clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a stable ochid target. This is why a bot-repo ochid names
`@-` (the last committed change), not `@`.

## .vc-config.toml

Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` whose `[repos]` registry records the workspace layout.
Values are ordinary paths relative to the config file's directory (absolute allowed,
discouraged), so the two sides' blocks **differ**: the entry that resolves to the config's own
directory names its side, and the two sides must agree on the same resolved work/bot pair:

```toml
# work side          # bot side
[repos]              [repos]
work = "."           work = ".."

## docs: always link the closing rung

- [[10]] 0.25.1 docs: always link the closing rung

### Problem

The closing rung was the ladder's one exception: unlinked until close-out gotchas gave it a
subsection, so a link's existence was unpredictable and the rung had no anchor while the cycle
ran. wink's template edit made the semicolon cycle practice the always-linked form, which left
TODO.md's shape template and three pinned statements contradicting each other.

### Solution

Every rung links 1:1 with a `Ladder details` subsection, closing included: the closing rung's
opens at laddering with a one-line stub and completes at close-out with gotchas in
problem/solution form, or `_None._`. Edited: the opening and close-out checklists, the
protocol's closing-rung paragraph, notes.md's slot note, prose.md's ladder-step surface, and
TODO.md's template description.

### Acceptance check

No agent-file states the unlinked-closing exception any more, and TODO.md's shape template
agrees with the checklists and the protocol.

**Result: passed**, 2026-08-14, by grep for the old exception's wording and by reading the
edited statements side by side. The grep earned its keep: it caught a fifth statement, in
prose.md's ladder-step surface, that the edit list had missed.

### Ladder

- [[N]] docs: always link the closing rung

### Deliberation

**Run as a single-commit cycle**, no entry moving to `## In Progress`, per the single-commit
form. The Todo "Change TODO rules so ladders 1:1 with detail" retires with it.

**The rule follows practice.** The semicolon cycle ran always-linked on wink's template edit,
and its closing subsection immediately earned its keep by holding the Concurrent-checkout
gotcha. The cost is a one-line stub per cycle.

**The protocol paragraph's tail was trimmed at review** (wink): the closing-rung paragraph had
accumulated a restatement of the chores move, a program-depth note, and a "still" comparing
against the old rule. The move and the depth shift are `Chores sections`' to state, and the
comparison is history, which this section now holds: the old rule created the closing
subsection only when gotchas occurred and left the rung unlinked until then. One detail
retires here with it, that under a program heading the subsections sit at markdown's heading
floor while the block is in `TODO.md`, which the shallower chores copy relieves.

**Recorded here for adjacency**: before this cycle's backfill, the landed 0.25.0 close-out was
re-described from the bare cycle title to the bookend form with " closing" (wink caught the
dropped suffix). A coordinated rewrite per the re-describe rule: the ochid trailer hand-copied,
both parents preserved, `main` force-pushed, and the backfill then recorded the rewritten SHA.
Residue: the pre-rewrite SHA 9f361686034e appears in this session's transcript, and this
sentence is its decoder.

## docs: propose dropping the depth-note paragraph

- [[N]] docs: propose dropping the depth-note paragraph

### Problem

wink asked for a three-way verification of the pinned set against `../vc-x1` and the template
payload, checking vc-x1's own report. It held: byte-identical throughout, except one four-line
paragraph of `cycle-protocol.md` present in their copy and the payload and absent from ours, the
same one-paragraph divergence the 2026-08-16 heads-up named as the whole member-to-member gap at
baseline. Left standing, every future sync re-raises it.

### Solution

Propose the deletion family-wide rather than adopt the paragraph. Our copy lacks it
deliberately: the paragraph is the tail of the old closing-rung paragraph, trimmed at the review
recorded in [docs: always link the closing rung](#docs-always-link-the-closing-rung), which
judged its first sentence a restatement of `Chores sections` and retired its program-depth note
to that section's records. vc-x1's trial rung adopted the replacement paragraph but kept the
tail as a standalone paragraph, and the template baseline took their copy. The proposal is the
template-repo branch `iiac-perf-drop-depth-note-paragraph`, one commit atop template `main`
deleting the paragraph, committed at wink's direction since the template is agent-less. This
section is the message body vc-x1's mailbox record points at.

### Acceptance check

The branch's diff against template `main` is exactly the paragraph deletion, and after it the
payload's `cycle-protocol.md` is byte-identical to our pinned copy.

**Result: passed**, 2026-08-18, by `diff` returning empty against our copy and `jj log` showing
the branch one commit ahead of an untouched `main`. The mailbox record follows this cycle's
push, on the durable-mode ordering (a permalink cannot precede the commit it names).

### Ladder

- [[N]] docs: propose dropping the depth-note paragraph

### Deliberation

**Relocation was the first plan, and the records killed it.** The depth note reads as the
paragraph's one non-redundant fact, so the agreed fix was folding it into `Chores sections`'
first transform bullet. Reading the always-link deliberation before editing showed wink had
already weighed that exact detail at review and retired it, so re-adding it would have quietly
reversed a reviewed decision. wink confirmed 2026-08-18 that the note covers nothing not
already covered elsewhere, and the fix became the deletion.

**The proposal rides a template branch, a first use.** The diff-is-proposal mechanism has no
purchase here: our copy already is the proposed state, so our diff against the payload shows
nothing to review, and a deletion proposal is invisible in exactly the mechanism built to carry
proposals. A branch on the template gives the proposal a neutral, stable home, its diff against
`main` being the proposal, with `main` moving only when the family accepts. Logged as a dogfood
entry pending the family's take.

**The bookmark carries the proposer's name** (`iiac-perf-` prefix) rather than the bare title
slug, so a branch listing shows whose proposal each branch is. wink reviewed the branch, its
commit, and the naming before this record was written.

1	# Code conventions
2	
3	Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
4	wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).
5	
6	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
7	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
8	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Line width
11	
12	Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
13	prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
14	The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
15	comment text it doesn't reflow.
16	
17	## Doc comments on every file, function, and method
18	
19	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
20	a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
21	is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
22	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
23	
24	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
25	inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected, while inline
26	explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
27	non-obvious WHY.
28	
29	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
30	by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
31	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
32	help.
33	
34	## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
35	
36	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
37	`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
38	patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
39	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
40	in scope:
41	
42	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
43	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
44	  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.
45	
46	When one is used, three obligations attach:
47	
48	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
49	  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
50	    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
51	  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
52	    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
53	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
54	    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
55	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
56	  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
57	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
58	  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:
59	
60	  ```toml
61	  [lints.clippy]
62	  unwrap_used = "warn"
63	  expect_used = "warn"
64	  ```
65	
66	  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
67	  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
68	  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
69	  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)
70	
71	```rust
72	let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
73	let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious
74	
75	match matches.len() {
76	    1 => {
77	        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
78	        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
79	        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
80	    }
81	    // ...
82	}
83	```
84	
85	Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
86	behavior.

[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected, while inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

1	//! Grading — two letters, answering two different questions.
2	//!
3	//! - [`RunGrade`] scores a measurement run from its own
4	//!   time-ordered [`BatchSummary`] series: how steady were *these
5	//!   numbers*, the ones being reported.
6	//! - [`EnvGrade`] scores the **box** from the warmup micro-probe
7	//!   series ([`ProbeSummary`]): how steady was the machine,
8	//!   measured on the apparatus alone before any workload entered
9	//!   the numbers.
10	//!
11	//! They share their arithmetic (signals scored against ascending
12	//! cutoffs, worst signal wins, every signal printing its own
13	//! letter) and deliberately not their thresholds or their signal
14	//! sets. A bench that reads F on the run grade and A on the
15	//! environment grade is a true and useful statement: the workload
16	//! is bursty on a quiet machine.
17	//!
18	//! Every signal is computed from the batches the run itself
19	//! produced, so the letter describes the data being reported
20	//! rather than a window measured beforehand.
21	//!
22	//! - Four signals, each scored against its own ascending cutoffs
23	//!   (A..F); the composite letter is the worst of them, and each
24	//!   signal prints its own letter beside its value so the
25	//!   composite always names its cause. See
26	//!   [`RunGrade::scores`] for the arithmetic and
27	//!   [`thresholds`] for the cutoffs.
28	//! - Four, where the startup calibration grade this replaced had
29	//!   six. Two of those six graded how well a *fit* held (a
30	//!   ladder point's residual against the Theil-Sen line, and the
31	//!   loop-only slope against the dithered two-point fit), and a
32	//!   bench run fits nothing: no line for a point to sit off, no
33	//!   second estimator to cross-check. Inventing a fit just to
34	//!   grade it would have been the wrong direction. The full
35	//!   mapping is recorded in
36	//!   notes/chores/chores-05.md#six-calibration-signals-four-run-signals.
37	//! - Two of the four watch the run's floor move under the
38	//!   measurement: `drift` asks whether the run ended where it
39	//!   began, `step` looks for a shift anywhere inside it and says
40	//!   when. A run that shifts and shifts back is invisible to the
41	//!   first and obvious to the second.
42	//! - The other two split contamination by how it is distributed:
43	//!   `interference` is the run-wide census rate (how many samples
44	//!   sat above their batch's floor), `bursts` the fraction of
45	//!   batches whose mean sits above the typical one (whether that
46	//!   interference was localized in time or spread evenly).
47	//!
48	//! The run grade **reports; it does not warn**. Its signals are facts
49	//! about the run, and a run's character is largely the workload's:
50	//! on a quiet 7600x the blocking mpsc round-trips read step F
51	//! whether pinned or not, while the same round-trip spinning reads
52	//! A — we think that is park/unpark bimodality, which belongs to
53	//! the bench, not the box. An F there is a true description of
54	//! what was measured, not a fault to raise, and the report's job
55	//! is a faithful histogram rather than a verdict. The verdict on
56	//! the box is a separate grade measured during warmup, where the
57	//! workload's character hasn't entered the numbers yet.
58	
59	use crate::harness::{BatchSummary, ProbeSummary};
60	
61	/// Grade thresholds, one array per signal: the ascending cutoffs
62	/// a signal crosses to score B, C, D, F (below the first is A).
63	///
64	/// - **Provisional** — seeded from the 3900X's quiet-run spread
65	///   on 2026-07-27 and checked against a quiet 7600x on
66	///   2026-07-28, where ten back-to-back `min-now` runs all read A
67	///   and 12 of 16 benches in one sweep read A.
68	/// - Calibrated on a fast single-threaded bench, where the run's
69	///   letter is mostly the box. A blocking multi-threaded bench
70	///   carries OS involvement in its own numbers and reads worse by
71	///   nature — correctly, since it *is* less steady. Nothing here
72	///   raises a warning, so a low letter costs a reader nothing
73	///   beyond the fact itself.
74	pub mod thresholds {
75	    /// Run-wide census rate: samples above their batch's
76	    /// over-floor cut, as a fraction of all samples.
77	    pub const INTERFERENCE: [f64; 4] = [0.02, 0.05, 0.12, 0.30];
78	    /// Fraction of batches whose mean sits [`super::BURST_TOL`] above the
79	    /// run's median batch mean.
80	    pub const BURSTS: [f64; 4] = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90];
81	    /// Floor movement from the run's first quarter to its last.
82	    pub const DRIFT: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
83	    /// Largest floor shift across any split of the run.
84	    pub const STEP: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
85	}
86	
87	/// Environment-grade thresholds — the same shape as
88	/// [`thresholds`], applied to the warmup micro-probe series.
89	///
90	/// - **Provisional**, and deliberately *not* shared with the run
91	///   grade even where the number happens to match: the two grade
92	///   different populations. A run's signals carry the workload's
93	///   character, a probe's carry only the box's, so the cutoffs
94	///   are free to diverge as measurement says they should.
95	/// - `drift` and `step` keep the run's cutoffs as a starting
96	///   point: both measure the same physical thing (floor movement
97	///   under the measurement), and the 3900X's ~9% bistable shift
98	///   sits well above the D cutoff either way.
99	pub mod env_thresholds {
100	    /// Probe spread: the p90-over-floor width of a typical probe.
101	    pub const SPREAD: [f64; 4] = [0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25];
102	    /// Census rate across the probe series: individual timer
103	    /// pairs above their probe's over-floor cut, as a fraction of
104	    /// all pairs. Counted per pair rather than per timed group
105	    /// because a group mean hides anything smaller than ~800 ns.
106	    ///
107	    /// - **The weakest of the four, and uncalibrated.** Set one
108	    ///   order of magnitude above the measured quiet baseline
109	    ///   (0.01% on a quiet 3900X) because there is no good upper
110	    ///   anchor: sharing the measured core with one spinner moved
111	    ///   it only to 0.04%, and with three spinners it read 0.01%
112	    ///   again. See
113	    ///   [`super::EnvGrade`]'s note on what the probe cannot see.
114	    pub const INTERFERENCE: [f64; 4] = [0.001, 0.005, 0.02, 0.05];
115	    /// Floor movement from the first quarter of warmup to the
116	    /// last — the frequency-ramp detector.
117	    pub const DRIFT: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
118	    /// Largest floor shift across any split of the warmup window.
119	    pub const STEP: [f64; 4] = [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10];
120	}
121	
122	/// A batch is "hot" when its mean exceeds the run's *median*
123	/// batch mean by this fraction — it carried something the typical
124	/// batch did not. The fraction of hot batches says whether the
125	/// contamination was localized in time or spread over the run.
126	///
127	/// - The reference is the median, not the quietest batch: the
128	///   minimum is an extreme, and against it a bench with any real
129	///   spread reads ~100% hot (mpsc-2t read 98% on a run whose
130	///   batch means varied normally).
131	pub const BURST_TOL: f64 = 0.05;
132	
133	/// Minimum batches on each side of a candidate split point for
134	/// the `step` detector to consider it. Below this a "transition"
135	/// is one or two batches — a burst, which the `bursts` signal
136	/// already counts.
137	pub const MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES: usize = 4;
138	
139	/// Score one signal against its [`thresholds`] array: 0 (A)
140	/// through 4 (F) — the count of cutoffs crossed.
141	fn score(x: f64, cutoffs: [f64; 4]) -> u8 {
142	    cutoffs.iter().filter(|&&c| x > c).count() as u8
143	}
144	
145	/// Map a 0..=4 score to its letter (no 'E': 4 is 'F').
146	fn score_letter(s: u8) -> char {
147	    match s {
148	        0 => 'A',
149	        1 => 'B',
150	        2 => 'C',
151	        3 => 'D',
152	        _ => 'F',
153	    }
154	}

content.text:
Ran the experiment that explains it: same box, same command, but pinned (`--pin 3`):

```
  env    warmup   4.07->4.09GHz 0.01s +-0.2%   A ...
```

The 4.8% collapses to 0.2% under a pin. That's the whole mystery:

**Why the 3900X reads `+-4.8%` unpinned.** The clock sampler reads `cpuinfo_avg_freq` of *whichever CPU the main thread happens to be on*. Unpinned, the scheduler moves it across your 24 CPUs during warmup, so the series mixes different cores running at different clocks. The 4.8% is not your clock wandering — it's a tour of the scheduler's placements. The 7600x run was presumably pinned (or just didn't migrate), so its series is one core's true story: climb 4.84→5.24, then genuinely flat, `+-0.0%`. So the two cells today are measuring different things, which is exactly why they "make no obvious sense" side by side.

**Why `0.01s`.** On this box under `powersave`, `min-now` never provokes a boost: the core sits at ~4.09GHz from the first probe, so the earliest settled suffix starts at probe 0 and its timestamp is 10ms. It's a true statement — "already at speed at the first look" — where the 7600x's `0.79s` is a real ramp being waited out. The two are the same measurement, just a box that has no journey versus one that does.

**What I'd fix — the sampling, not the presentation:** filter every clock statistic (start, settled median, rating, and the `-v` min/max/ticks) to the **dominant CPU's samples** — the core that provided the most readings. Then an unpinned run reports one core's story instead of a scheduler tour, and your two boxes become directly comparable and self-explanatory:

- 3900X: `4.09->4.09GHz 0.01s +-0.2%` — "never moved, steady within 10ms, held to 0.2%"
- 7600x: `4.84->5.24GHz 0.79s +-0.0%` — "climbed for 0.79s, then dead flat"

On your two other suggestions, my take:

- **Range (min-max) instead of start->end**: the `-v` clock line already carries `(min 3.58 max 4.11)`, and the arrow carries direction, which range loses — a throttling box that fell would read the same as one that climbed. After the dominant-CPU fix, start->end and min-max nearly coincide anyway on healthy runs. I'd keep the arrow in the cell and the range in `-v`.
- **A grade letter instead of the %**: possible (anchored on the 1% stability tolerance), but the report's philosophy has been "the clock column reports, the letters judge timing" — and after the fix the % is small, honest, and self-scaling. I'd hold the letter until real runs show the % needs interpreting.

The plain version: the weird 4.8% was the measurement following your program around as the scheduler moved it between cores, not the clock misbehaving — pinning proves it, reading 0.2%. The 10ms just means "this box was already at speed when we first looked", while the 7600x genuinely spent 0.79 seconds climbing. If I make the clock statistics stick to the one core that was sampled most, both boxes' cells become directly comparable with no special cases. Want me to make that change (dominant-CPU filtering) as part of this rung?

content.content:
### Settle time

The warmup row's `settle` cell says how long the box took to
settle: `0.86s`, or `not settled` when it was still moving
when warmup ended. It exists because warmup now *absorbs* the
box coming up to speed rather than being graded on it: the first
run of a process spends `--settle-time` seconds (default 1.5)
stepping the bench before recording anything, so the letter
answers "was it settled when measurement started" and this
answers "how long did that take".

The warm is per **process**, not per bench: the boost it wins is
machine state, so every later bench in the same process inherits
it. Without it the first bench of a process reports a cold
machine's numbers (measured at ~8.6% slow on a 7600x, a wrong
histogram rather than merely a wrong letter) while benches 2..N
read correctly. Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep.

Settle time is *when the floor entered, and stayed inside, ±1% of
the level warmup ended at*. Precisely: each probe's floor is its
p10 group cost; the settled level is the median floor over the
300 ms tail window; a running 8-probe median (a quarter of the
series when it is shorter than that, matching what `drift`
compares) has to sit inside the band; the reported time is the
probe after the last one that didn't; and that state has to hold
through the whole tail window, or the reading is `not settled`.

That last requirement is what keeps the number about the box
rather than about the budget. Settle is the last excursion's end,
so on a machine that keeps flickering the last excursion is near

### Settle time

The warmup row's `settle` cell says how long the box took to
settle: `0.86s`, or `not settled` when it was still moving
when warmup ended. It exists because warmup now *absorbs* the
box coming up to speed rather than being graded on it: the first
run of a process spends `--settle-time` seconds (default 1.5)
stepping the bench before recording anything, so the letter
answers "was it settled when measurement started" and this
answers "how long did that take".

The warm is per **process**, not per bench: the boost it wins is
machine state, so every later bench in the same process inherits
it. Without it the first bench of a process reports a cold
machine's numbers (measured at ~8.6% slow on a 7600x, a wrong
histogram rather than merely a wrong letter) while benches 2..N
read correctly. Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep.

Settle time is *when the floor entered, and stayed inside, ±1% of
the level warmup ended at*. Precisely: each probe's floor is its
p10 group cost; the settled level is the median floor over the
300 ms tail window; a running 8-probe median (a quarter of the
series when it is shorter than that, matching what `drift`
compares) has to sit inside the band; the reported time is the
probe after the last one that didn't; and that state has to hold
through the whole tail window, or the reading is `not settled`.

That last requirement is what keeps the number about the box
rather than about the budget. Settle is the last excursion's end,
so on a machine that keeps flickering the last excursion is near
the end of warmup *whenever warmup ends*: on a 3900X,
`--settle-time 1.5` reported a ~1.0 s median settle and
`--settle-time 5` a 4.63 s one, same box, same state. Demanding
that the state hold through the graded window makes "settled at
T" mean the box actually stayed there.

Two things it does not say: it is measured against where *this*
warmup ended, not any absolute best speed, so it never says which

---

**The settle cell**

The warmup row's `settle` cell is the story of the CPU clock
during warmup, read left to right:

```
4.07->4.54GHz 1.60s +-11.9%
```

- `4.07->4.54GHz` — the journey: the delivered clock at the
  first reading, and the level the box settled at (the median
  of the settled stretch). An arrow that goes nowhere
  (`4.09->4.09GHz`) is a box that was already at speed.
- `1.60s` — the settle time: how much warmup passed before
  timing and clock both held still from there on. Everything
  the report grades and measures ran after this point.
  `<0.01s` means the first look already saw the settled state:
  no observed warm-up was needed.
- `+-11.9%` — steadiness: the relative standard deviation of
  the clock across the settled stretch. A pinned clock
  certifies itself here (`+-0.0%`); a governor still wandering
  shows a fatter band.

Other forms: `4.07->4.54GHz not settled` is a box still moving
when warmup gave up (the numbers that follow were measured on a
moving clock). A cell with no GHz (`0.32s`, `from start`,
`not settled`) is a driver that exposes no readable clock.

---

Two things this drafting exercise exposed, and they're why I stopped short of writing it into the README:

1. **The `+-11.9%` fails the explanation test.** The honest footnote for today's implementation would have to say: "unpinned, these numbers describe whichever cores the scheduler moved the sampler across, not your clock" — which is an admission, not an explanation. It's also why the same box read +-4.8%, then +-0.2% pinned, now +-11.9%: the number is mostly scheduler placement. With the dominant-CPU filter (stats computed over the single most-sampled core), the number becomes one core's truth, run-to-run comparable, and the text above needs no footnote.
2. **The `0.01s` becomes explainable with one character.** Printed as `<0.01s`, it says what is actually true: the settle time is below what we can observe, because the first probe (10ms in) already saw the settled state. "How much warmup did this box need" → "less than 10ms". That's your "total settle time" reading, with the censoring marked instead of dressed as a measurement.

On slope: the journey and the time already imply it (0.47GHz over 1.60s), so I'd not spend a fourth number on it.

So my proposal for finishing this rung: dominant-CPU filtering plus the `<` censoring mark, then the README text above matches reality with no asterisks. And you're right that every column eventually needs this treatment — I'd put "document every report column/line in README" in as a Todo entry rather than grow this rung further.

The plain version: the cell's three parts are "where the clock went, how long that took, and how steady it stayed". The confusing numbers you saw are real defects: the percentage today mixes different CPU cores when the run isn't pinned, and the ten-millisecond time is really "faster than we could see". does not qualify. Use it to characterize a box before trusting
numbers from it.

What it runs is, in metrology terms, a repeatability study of the
apparatus plus the machine, which is why the grading module is
called `gauge`.

```
  run   warmup  bench    worst   settle   mean
  1     A       A        A       0.86s    22.2 ns
  2     D       A        D       1.31s    22.2 ns
  3     A       C        C       0.61s    22.5 ns

  median environment grade: A
  median settle: 0.86s (0 of 3 never settled)
  transition-degraded (drift or step at D/F): 1 of 3

  verdict: NOT QUALIFIED
    a state transition landed inside a measurement window
```

It reads the environment grade rather than the run grade,
because the subject is the box: `warmup` is its settling
behaviour across respawns, `bench` whether it then held. The
verdict is grades, not values: median at B or better, and no
run whose `drift` or `step` reached D/F, those two being the
transition detectors. `spread` and `interference` wobble is
ambient contamination and does not fail a run. The `mean` column
is informational, and it is where a two-state machine shows
itself at a glance.

The `settle` column is how long each child's warmup took to
reach the state it measured in (`not` when it never did; see
[Settle time](#settle-time)). It is reported, not judged: a box
still moving when warmup ended already shows up as a `drift` or
`step` D/F on the warmup stretch, so a second criterion would
only restate the first. What it adds is the size of the number:
how much `--settle-time` this box actually wants.

Each child runs `min-now` for `-d` seconds (default 1): the box
is the subject, so the leanest bench is the right one. `--pin`
and `--settle-time` pass through to the children, and
`--print-only` prints the table without deciding a verdict.

carapace completion spec: Tab then completes bench names, command

### The two grades

Every report ends with the grade block: one column header over
three rows, each graded A-F from its own data: two `env` rows
for the **box**, one `run` row for *that run*. A row's `worst`
column is its composite, printed beside the signals that earned
it; a blank cell (`-`) means that signal does not apply to that
row, which is the env/run signal mapping made visible:

```
  grade  phase        settle  worst     spread  bursts  interference      drift               step
  env    warmup        0.86s      A    0.47% A       -       0.00% A    0.00% A            0.00% A
  env    bench             -      F    0.48% A       -       0.00% A   11.05% F    11.05% @1.06s F
  run    all               -      F          -   37% B       0.04% A   10.49% F    10.49% @1.04s F
```

Column reference (each signal prints its own letter beside its
value; the sections below carry the depth):

- `grade` / `phase`: row labels. The two `env` rows grade the
  box from micro-probes that never touch the bench (`warmup`:
  did it end settled; `bench`: did it stay settled). The `run`
  row grades the numbers above it, from the run's own batches.
- `settle`: warmup row only. How long the box took to settle,
  or `not settled`; see [Settle time](#settle-time).
- `worst`: the row's composite letter, its worst signal
  outright; always one of the letters printed beside it.
- `spread`: env rows only. How wide a probe's bulk sits above
  its own floor. A timer pair has no workload character, so
  width means the box itself moved.
- `bursts`: run row only. The fraction of batches whose mean
  sits above the run's median batch: whether interference was
  localized in time or spread out.
- `interference`: samples that sat above their batch's floor,
  as a fraction of the run: how much other work leaked in.
- `drift`: floor movement from the run's first quarter to its

Two things it does not say: it is measured against where *this*
warmup ended, not any absolute best speed, so it never says which
state was the right one; and it is biased early by up to one
window, since the first window that reads settled straddles the
last of the ramp.

`--settle-time 0` skips the warm, which is how you measure what
it is worth on a given box. A box that reads `not settled` at
the default wants more, though that is not always curable: on a
3900X the floor is bistable and moves at arbitrary times, so a
3.5 s warm still left runs moving mid-bench. Replication
(`--blocks`) is the answer there, not a longer warm.

The probes run through warmup and then in the seam at every batch
boundary, so the series covers the whole run on the same time
axis as the batches. `--no-env-probe` limits them to warmup (so
only the warmup row appears),
which costs the grade its span; it exists because seam probing
perturbs a spinning multi-threaded bench by ~0.9% (measured on
`zcr-with-2t`), a bias that is common-mode in an A/B between two
benches but not in an absolute number.

pair has no character of its own. Note that `env interference`
is the weakest of the four: a probe measures the box only while

The warmup row's `settle` cell says how long the box took to
settle: `0.86s`, or `not settled` when it was still moving
when warmup ended. It exists because warmup now *absorbs* the
box coming up to speed rather than being graded on it: the first

input.new_string:
### Settle time

The warmup row's `settle` cell is the story of the CPU clock
during warmup, read left to right:

```
4.84->5.24GHz held 0.73s +-0.0%
```

- `4.84->5.24GHz`: the journey, the delivered clock at the
  first reading and the state it settled into (the median of
  the settled stretch). An arrow that goes nowhere
  (`4.09->4.09GHz`) is a box that was already at speed.
- `held 0.73s`: how long the settled state held before
  measurement began. A box settled through the whole warm
  holds the budget the setup banner names (`held 1.51s` under
  `settle 1.5s`), and a short hold is a box that spent most of
  its warm still moving.
- `+-0.0%`: how still "settled" is, the relative standard
  deviation of the clock across the settled stretch. A pinned
  clock certifies itself here, and a governor still wandering
  shows a fatter band.

`4.07->4.54GHz not settled` is a box still moving when warmup
gave up (a hold of zero): the numbers that follow were measured
on a moving clock. A cell with no GHz (`held 0.73s` alone) is a
driver that exposes no readable delivered clock.

"Settled" means what the warm exit means: from some point on,
the probe timings grade A *and* the delivered clock held inside
1%. The cell reports the earliest such point: the journey ends
at it, the hold runs from it to the end of warmup, and the
steadiness is measured across it. Every clock number reads the
single most-sampled CPU, because an unpinned run's sampler
rides the scheduler across cores and a mixed series rates
placement rather than the clock (measured on a 3900X: +-11.9%
mixed against +-0.2% for the same box filtered or pinned). It
never says which state was the *right* one: the journey is
measured against where this warmup ended, not any absolute
best speed.

`-v` adds a `clock:` line under the warmup probe table: the
journey, one tick per clock step (`^`/`v` a move beyond the 1%
band, `-` a hold inside it), and the series extremes. The
settled stretch reads all `-` by construction, so the settle
point is visible as the place the ticks go quiet.

The cell exists because warmup *absorbs* the box coming up to
speed rather than being graded on it: the first run of a
process spends `--settle-time` seconds (default 1.5) stepping
the bench before recording anything, so the letter answers "was
it settled when measurement started" and this cell answers "at
what state, and settled for how long".

content.content:
process spends `--settle-time` seconds (default 1.5) stepping
the bench before recording anything, so the letter answers "was
it settled when measurement started" and this cell answers "at
what state, and settled for how long".

The warm is per **process**, not per bench: the boost it wins is
machine state, so every later bench in the same process inherits
it. Without it the first bench of a process reports a cold
machine's numbers (measured at ~8.6% slow on a 7600x, a wrong
histogram rather than merely a wrong letter) while benches 2..N
read correctly. Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep.

Settle time is *when the floor entered, and stayed inside, ±1% of
the level warmup ended at*. Precisely: each probe's floor is its
p10 group cost; the settled level is the median floor over the
300 ms tail window; a running 8-probe median (a quarter of the
series when it is shorter than that, matching what `drift`
compares) has to sit inside the band; the reported time is the
probe after the last one that didn't; and that state has to hold
through the whole tail window, or the reading is `not settled`.

That last requirement is what keeps the number about the box
rather than about the budget. Settle is the last excursion's end,
so on a machine that keeps flickering the last excursion is near
the end of warmup *whenever warmup ends*: on a 3900X,
`--settle-time 1.5` reported a ~1.0 s median settle and
`--settle-time 5` a 4.63 s one, same box, same state. Demanding
that the state hold through the graded window makes "settled at
T" mean the box actually stayed there.

Two things it does not say: it is measured against where *this*
warmup ended, not any absolute best speed, so it never says which
state was the right one; and it is biased early by up to one
window, since the first window that reads settled straddles the
last of the ramp.

`--settle-time 0` skips the warm, which is how you measure what

input.old_string:
As landed, the conceptual delta:

- `Settle` carries the journey rather than a scan timestamp: `At` gains `from_start`,
  `start_ghz`, and `rating`, `Never` gains its two journey ends, and the record schema is
  untouched (`settle_s` / `settle_ghz` keep their meaning, the journey being a report surface)
- the spec's no-change form dropped at review (wink): a journey that went nowhere still prints
  its arrow and time, `4.09->4.09GHz 0.01s +-0.2%`, keeping the column uniform across boxes
  (the 7600x's moved form beside the 3900X's flat one). `from start` survives only in the
  timing-only form, where there is no journey to show
- the rating exposes what the gate's fallbacks hide: measured live, an unpinned child read
  `3.72->4.09GHz 0.01s +-4.0%`, the CPU-migration fallback in `clock_stable` waving an
  uncertifiable climb through while the rating shows the spread. The fatter band the spec
  predicted for `powersave` is real and visible
- the report's unstable-exit arm now prints the scan's `Never` journey instead of a bare
  `not settled`, with the plain form kept as the defensive fallback

1	//! Grading — two letters, answering two different questions.
2	//!
3	//! - [`RunGrade`] scores a measurement run from its own
4	//!   time-ordered [`BatchSummary`] series: how steady were *these
5	//!   numbers*, the ones being reported.
6	//! - [`EnvGrade`] scores the **box** from the warmup micro-probe
7	//!   series ([`ProbeSummary`]): how steady was the machine,
8	//!   measured on the apparatus alone before any workload entered
9	//!   the numbers.
10	//!
11	//! They share their arithmetic (signals scored against ascending
12	//! cutoffs, worst signal wins, every signal printing its own
13	//! letter) and deliberately not their thresholds or their signal
14	//! sets. A bench that reads F on the run grade and A on the
15	//! environment grade is a true and useful statement: the workload
16	//! is bursty on a quiet machine.
17	//!
18	//! Every signal is computed from the batches the run itself
19	//! produced, so the letter describes the data being reported
20	//! rather than a window measured beforehand.
21	//!
22	//! - Four signals, each scored against its own ascending cutoffs
23	//!   (A..F); the composite letter is the worst of them, and each
24	//!   signal prints its own letter beside its value so the
25	//!   composite always names its cause. See
26	//!   [`RunGrade::scores`] for the arithmetic and
27	//!   [`thresholds`] for the cutoffs.
28	//! - Four, where the startup calibration grade this replaced had
29	//!   six. Two of those six graded how well a *fit* held (a
30	//!   ladder point's residual against the Theil-Sen line, and the
31	//!   loop-only slope against the dithered two-point fit), and a
32	//!   bench run fits nothing: no line for a point to sit off, no
33	//!   second estimator to cross-check. Inventing a fit just to
34	//!   grade it would have been the wrong direction. The full
35	//!   mapping is recorded in
36	//!   notes/chores/chores-05.md#six-calibration-signals-four-run-signals.
37	//! - Two of the four watch the run's floor move under the
38	//!   measurement: `drift` asks whether the run ended where it
39	//!   began, `step` looks for a shift anywhere inside it and says
40	//!   when. A run that shifts and shifts back is invisible to the

42	//! - The other two split contamination by how it is distributed:
43	//!   `interference` is the run-wide census rate (how many samples

content.text:
Fixed and validated (fmt, clippy, 119 tests, install) — please review. What your odd row was, and what changed:

**Your row explained.** `warmup A` beside `not settled` is the designed honest pairing: the warmup letter grades *timing* over the exit window, and this box's timing looks fine while its clock is still moving — the exact defect this rung exists to expose. What was wrong was the *bare* `not settled` with no journey on a box whose clock is perfectly readable.

**The root cause** was my dominant-CPU filter interacting badly with the shared gate: filtering turns other cores' samples into `None`, and `clock_stable`'s missing-sample fallback returns `true` at the first `None` it meets — so on unpinned runs the scan's clock gate was effectively disabled. That's also what produced the `+-7.0%` rating inside a supposedly 1% gate in my reproduction, and the GHz-less cells on short warmups.

**The fix**: the scan now uses its own `filtered_clock_stable`, the same 1% band but ranging over the dominant core's *readable* samples and skipping the gaps (post-filter, a `None` just means "sampled elsewhere at that probe", not "no honest series"). The `Never` journey's end also falls back to the last readable sample when the exit window held none, which is what had emptied your row's journey. The warm-exit gate itself is untouched.

After the fix, five unpinned qualify runs on this box read:

```
  1     A       A        A       4.07->4.49GHz not settled   28.3 ns
  2     A       A        A       4.07->4.47GHz 0.05s +-0.2%  28.2 ns
  3     A       D        D       4.48->4.49GHz 0.85s +-0.2%  27.5 ns
  5     A       C        C       3.89->4.09GHz 0.92s +-0.2%  28.1 ns
```

Every rating tight, every journey present, and the box's real two-regime character (4.09 vs 4.47-4.49 settle states wandering run to run) visible in the settle column — which is what the qualify table was always supposed to show. A regression test pins the gap-wandering case, and the TODO record and README's no-GHz sentence are updated.

content.text:
Both observations are the same design seam, and it's worth deciding deliberately. Here's what's happening and where I think the fix belongs:

**Why `A` sits beside `not settled`.** The warmup letter grades *timing*: the probe floors and spreads over the exit window. The clock gate was deliberately kept out of the letter — grades stay facts about measured time, and the clock is "read, never scored" — so a box whose timing held still while its clock was mid-climb reads A on timing and `not settled` on the clock. On this box that combination is real, not a bug: the floor genuinely didn't move during those windows even though the clock hadn't finished its journey.

**But your table exposes a leak in the old justification.** The documented argument for keeping settle out of the verdict was "a box still moving at warmup's end shows up as drift/step D/F anyway, so a second criterion would only restate the first." Runs 4, 6, 7 support that — their moves landed in the bench and got caught. Runs 2 and 10 refute it: `not settled` at warmup's end, and the bench row still graded A/B, presumably because the ramp completed inside the first few batches where the drift quarter-comparison and the step detector's minimum split can't see it. So a fast late ramp can slip past every timing detector, and the only witness is the settle cell — which currently has no vote in the verdict.

**My recommendation, in two parts:**

1. **Keep the warmup letter timing-pure.** It honestly grades what it measures, and muddying it would break "the composite always names its cause" (an F with all-A signals beside it would need a footnote).
2. **Give `not settled` a vote in qualify's *verdict*** — qualify is exactly the command whose job is "is this box fit to measure on", and a box that can't finish its clock journey inside the warm budget isn't, whether or not the timing detectors happened to catch the move. Concretely: `never settled` runs count as transition-degraded (or a separate disqualifier line: "3 of 10 never settled" already prints, it just doesn't decide anything).

Scope-wise this is verdict logic, not cell format, and the next rung — `feat: qualify-environment reads the power policy` — is precisely about qualify's fitness preconditions. I'd fold "not settled disqualifies" into that rung's spec rather than stretch this one further; this rung's deliverable (the cell tells the truth) is what just made the leak visible at all.

One aside from your run: rows 5, 8, 9 show *downward* journeys (`4.52->4.49GHz`) — boost decaying toward sustained, another true story the arrow now carries.

Want me to add the not-settled-disqualifies bullet to the qualify rung's spec in TODO.md, and then this rung is ready for its commit description?

content.text:
Added to the README's settle section, right on the hold bullet.

The plain version: the harness stops warming as soon as it sees fifty milliseconds of calm. A machine that's restless until the very end therefore always shows exactly those fifty milliseconds — `0.05s` — because calm and "stop warming" arrive together. Only a machine that calmed down early can show a bigger number, up to the full warm budget like your run 1's `1.50s`. So the settle column now reads as three regimes: `1.50s` (was ready all along), something in between (took a while, then held), and `0.05s` (barely made it) — with `not settled` as the fourth (never made it).

Still pending from the previous turn: your call on adding "`not settled` disqualifies" to the qualify rung's spec, and then this rung is ready for its commit description.

Column reference (each signal prints its own letter beside its
value; the sections below carry the depth):

- `grade` / `phase`: row labels. The two `env` rows grade the

  row grades the numbers above it, from the run's own batches.

  that state held before measurement began, and how still it
  held, or `not settled`; see [Settle time](#settle-time).

  outright; always one of the letters printed beside it.
- `spread`: env rows only. How wide a probe's bulk sits above
  its own floor. A timer pair has no workload character, so
  width means the box itself moved.
- `bursts`: run row only. The fraction of batches whose mean
  sits above the run's median batch: whether interference was
  localized in time or spread out.

input.description: Read the settle section as it stands

content.content:
The warmup row's `settle` cell is the story of the CPU clock
during warmup, read left to right:

```
4.84->5.24GHz 0.73s +-0.0%
```

- `4.84->5.24GHz`: the journey, the delivered clock at the
  first reading and the state it settled into (the median of
  the settled stretch). An arrow that goes nowhere
  (`4.09->4.09GHz`) is a box that was already at speed.
- `0.73s`: the settle time, how long the settled state held
  before measurement began. A box settled through the whole
  warm holds the budget the setup banner names (`1.50s` under
  `settle 1.5s`), and a short hold is a box that spent most of
  its warm still moving. The hold has a floor: warmup exits
  the moment its trailing window (at least 50 ms) reads
  settled, so a box still moving until the end settles just in
  time and reads exactly that floor. A recurring `0.05s` is
  the floor itself: settled at the last possible moment,
  certified by the minimum window and nothing more.
- `+-0.0%`: how still "settled" is, the relative standard
  deviation of the clock across the settled stretch. A pinned
  clock certifies itself here, and a governor still wandering
  shows a fatter band.

`4.07->4.54GHz not settled` is a box still moving when warmup
gave up (a hold of zero): the numbers that follow were measured
on a moving clock. A cell with no GHz (`0.73s` alone) is a run
whose clock had no readable story: a driver without a delivered
clock, or a thread never sampled long enough on one core.

1%. The cell reports the earliest such point: the journey ends

histogram rather than merely a wrong letter) while benches 2..N
read correctly. Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep.

1	//! Grading — two letters, answering two different questions.
2	//!
3	//! - [`RunGrade`] scores a measurement run from its own
4	//!   time-ordered [`BatchSummary`] series: how steady were *these
5	//!   numbers*, the ones being reported.
6	//! - [`EnvGrade`] scores the **box** from the warmup micro-probe
7	//!   series ([`ProbeSummary`]): how steady was the machine,
8	//!   measured on the apparatus alone before any workload entered
9	//!   the numbers.
10	//!
11	//! They share their arithmetic (signals scored against ascending
12	//! cutoffs, worst signal wins, every signal printing its own
13	//! letter) and deliberately not their thresholds or their signal
14	//! sets. A bench that reads F on the run grade and A on the
15	//! environment grade is a true and useful statement: the workload
16	//! is bursty on a quiet machine.
17	//!
18	//! Every signal is computed from the batches the run itself
19	//! produced, so the letter describes the data being reported
20	//! rather than a window measured beforehand.
21	//!
22	//! - Four signals, each scored against its own ascending cutoffs
23	//!   (A..F); the composite letter is the worst of them, and each
24	//!   signal prints its own letter beside its value so the
25	//!   composite always names its cause. See
26	//!   [`RunGrade::scores`] for the arithmetic and
27	//!   [`thresholds`] for the cutoffs.
28	//! - Four, where the startup calibration grade this replaced had
29	//!   six. Two of those six graded how well a *fit* held (a
30	//!   ladder point's residual against the Theil-Sen line, and the
31	//!   loop-only slope against the dithered two-point fit), and a
32	//!   bench run fits nothing: no line for a point to sit off, no
33	//!   second estimator to cross-check. Inventing a fit just to
34	//!   grade it would have been the wrong direction. The full
35	//!   mapping is recorded in
36	//!   notes/chores/chores-05.md#six-calibration-signals-four-run-signals.
37	//! - Two of the four watch the run's floor move under the
38	//!   measurement: `drift` asks whether the run ended where it
39	//!   began, `step` looks for a shift anywhere inside it and says
40	//!   when. A run that shifts and shifts back is invisible to the
41	//!   first and obvious to the second.
42	//! - The other two split contamination by how it is distributed:
43	//!   `interference` is the run-wide census rate (how many samples
44	//!   sat above their batch's floor), `bursts` the fraction of
45	//!   batches whose mean sits above the typical one (whether that
46	//!   interference was localized in time or spread evenly).
47	//!
48	//! The run grade **reports; it does not warn**. Its signals are facts
49	//! about the run, and a run's character is largely the workload's:
50	//! on a quiet 7600x the blocking mpsc round-trips read step F
51	//! whether pinned or not, while the same round-trip spinning reads
52	//! A — we think that is park/unpark bimodality, which belongs to
53	//! the bench, not the box. An F there is a true description of
54	//! what was measured, not a fault to raise, and the report's job
55	//! is a faithful histogram rather than a verdict. The verdict on
56	//! the box is a separate grade measured during warmup, where the
57	//! workload's character hasn't entered the numbers yet.

62	/// a signal crosses to score B, C, D, F (below the first is A).
63	///
64	/// - **Provisional** — seeded from the 3900X's quiet-run spread
65	///   on 2026-07-27 and checked against a quiet 7600x on
66	///   2026-07-28, where ten back-to-back `min-now` runs all read A
67	///   and 12 of 16 benches in one sweep read A.
68	/// - Calibrated on a fast single-threaded bench, where the run's
69	///   letter is mostly the box. A blocking multi-threaded bench
70	///   carries OS involvement in its own numbers and reads worse by

72	///   raises a warning, so a low letter costs a reader nothing
73	///   beyond the fact itself.
74	pub mod thresholds {
75	    /// Run-wide census rate: samples above their batch's
76	    /// over-floor cut, as a fraction of all samples.
77	    pub const INTERFERENCE: [f64; 4] = [0.02, 0.05, 0.12, 0.30];
78	    /// Fraction of batches whose mean sits [`super::BURST_TOL`] above the

- `49%`: the settled share of the warm, how much of warmup was
  spent in the settled state. `100%` is a box that was ready
  all along, a small share is one that settled at the last
  moment (the floor is the exit window, at least 50 ms, as a
  share of the warm, since warmup exits the moment that window
  reads settled), and `0%` is reserved for never settled: a
  settled share always rounds up to at least `1%`.
- `+-0.0%`: how still "settled" is, the relative standard
  deviation of the clock across the settled stretch. A pinned
  clock certifies itself here, and a governor still wandering
  shows a fatter band.

no share of the warm was certified, the numbers that follow
were measured on a moving clock, and the warmup row's `worst`

grade: a fast late ramp can finish inside the bench's first
batches where no timing detector sees it, so the settle scan is
the only witness that the box was not fit. A cell with no GHz
(`49%` alone) is a run whose clock had no readable story: a
driver without a delivered clock, or a thread never sampled
long enough on one core.
