1	# iiac-perf
2	
3	A general-purpose latency microbenchmark harness for Rust. Each
4	bench runs against a wall-clock time budget with auto-sized loop
5	counts and reports a percentile-band histogram in nanoseconds.
6	
7	Numbers are raw: nothing is subtracted, so a column is what the
8	apparatus measured. The apparatus does cost something (a timer
9	pair plus the loop that drives it), and the inner loop is sized
10	so that cost is a small fraction of the workload's, which is what
11	makes a raw number usable rather than merely honest. What the
12	harness will not do is estimate that cost and subtract it: the
13	estimate is ill-defined at this scale, and it cancels anyway in
14	the same-harness A/B comparison the tool exists for.
15	
16	Highlights:
17	
18	- Time-based runs (`-d SECONDS` per bench, `-D SECONDS` total)
19	  with auto-sized outer/inner loop counts.
20	- Band-based histogram (min->p1, p1->p10, ..., p99->max) with count,
21	  mean, and range.
22	- Per-run grades for the workload and for the machine, each
23	  computed from the run's own data.
24	- Per-thread CPU pinning (`--pin`): thread 0 of a bench measures
25	  on main, which pins to the pool's first slot; the warm loop
26	  runs there too, so the frequency state it wins lands on the
27	  core that measures.
28	- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
29	  registering in `src/benches/`.
30	
31	The first benches measure Inter-Intra Application Communication
32	(function calls, async calls, channels, serde), which is what
33	seeded the project name. The harness itself is workload-agnostic.
34	The `ice-*` benches measure iceoryx2 shared-memory IPC inside one
35	process, in both of its messaging patterns (`ice-ps-*`
36	publish/subscribe, `ice-rr-*` request/response) at one and two
37	threads.
38	
39	## Design (0.2.0)
40	
41	Design a Rust app that can measure the cost of various (IIAC) techniques.
42	By IIAC I mean all communication techniques between and within
43	applications such as regular function calls vs async function calls vs
44	channels vs serde/deser of json or zero-copy messaging using io_uring and
45	potentially any other technique. It would include between threads or
46	processes or apps on the same computer or between apps on the same LAN or
47	between apps over a WAN.
48	
49	Ideally I'd like to be able to see a histogram of the range of times of the
50	send and receive costs, not just the mean/average of 10^3 or 10^6 invocations.
51	So the cost of the work should or could be something near-zero such as just
52	echoing the input, but maybe there is value in doing some constant but
53	variable amount of work to verify it's in-consequential. One thing I think we
54	need to be aware of is that if we make the work too simple the compiler could
55	just keep things in registers which would not be representative of "real" work.
56	
57	We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
58	later expand to other techniques.
59	
60	## Usage
61	
62	```
63	iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
64	iiac-perf qualify-environment [--runs N] [--gap SECONDS] [-d SECONDS]
65	iiac-perf add-completion-yaml
66	```
67	
68	`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
69	registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
70	bench it is a prefix of: `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
71	runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
72	available list and exits, and that's the source of truth for which
73	benches the current build registers.**
74	
75	`iiac-perf qualify-environment` (also stand-alone) asks whether
76	this **machine** is fit to measure on:
77	it respawns this binary `--runs` times (default 10) at `--gap`
78	seconds apart, collects each run's environment grade, prints the
79	table, and gives a verdict, exiting nonzero when the machine
80	does not qualify. Use it to characterize a box before trusting
81	numbers from it.
82	
83	What it runs is, in metrology terms, a repeatability study of the
84	apparatus plus the machine, which is why the grading module is
85	called `gauge`.
86	
87	```
88	  run   warmup  bench    worst   settle                      mean
89	  1     A       A        A       4.84->5.24GHz 49% +-0.0%    22.2 ns
90	  2     B       A        B       4.84->5.24GHz 18% +-0.1%    22.2 ns
91	  3     F       C        F       4.85->5.24GHz 00%           22.5 ns
92	
93	  median environment grade: B
94	  median settled: 18% of warmup (1 of 3 never settled)
95	  transition-degraded (drift or step at D/F): 1 of 3
96	
97	  verdict: NOT QUALIFIED
98	    a state transition landed inside a measurement window
99	```
100	
101	It reads the environment grade rather than the run grade,
102	because the subject is the box: `warmup` is its settling
103	behaviour across respawns, `bench` whether it then held. The
104	verdict is grades, not values: median at B or better, and no
105	run whose `drift` or `step` reached D/F, those two being the
106	transition detectors. `spread` and `interference` wobble is
107	ambient contamination and does not fail a run. The `mean` column
108	is informational, and it is where a two-state machine shows
109	itself at a glance.
110	
111	The `settle` column is each child warmup's clock journey and
112	settled share (`00%` with a warmup F when it never settled; see
113	[Settle time](#settle-time)). The states themselves are the
114	fastest read on a two-state box: which clock each run measured
115	at, and a small share is a box that wants more `--settle-time`
116	than it got.
117	
118	Each child runs `min-now` for `-d` seconds (default 1): the box
119	is the subject, so the leanest bench is the right one. `--pin`
120	and `--settle-time` pass through to the children, and
121	`--print-only` prints the table without deciding a verdict.
122	
123	`iiac-perf add-completion-yaml` (also stand-alone) installs the
124	carapace completion spec: Tab then completes bench names, command
125	words, and flags in any carapace-served shell. Without it,
126	`iiac-perf ice<TAB>` has nothing to offer and bench names must
127	be typed (or copied from the no-args listing) by hand. Run it
128	once after installing iiac-perf, and again after an upgrade
129	that changes flags or command words; new benches never need a
130	re-run. See [Shell completion](#shell-completion).
131	
132	Flags (also visible via `-h` / `--help`):
133	- `-d`, `--duration SECONDS`: target wall-clock seconds per bench
134	  (default `5.0`); the outer loop runs until this time is reached
135	  (inner auto-sizes). See chores `0.3.1-dev1` for the empirical
136	  study behind the default; longer (`-d 30`+) gives
137	  publication-grade stability. Mutually exclusive with `-D`.
138	- `-D`, `--total-duration SECONDS`: target total wall-clock seconds
139	  across all requested benches; budget is split equally per bench
140	  (e.g. `-D 30` with 6 benches -> 5 s each). Mutually exclusive with
141	  `-d`.
142	- `-o`, `--outer N`: override outer loop count (forces count-based
143	  mode instead of time-based; inner still adapts).
144	- `-i`, `--inner N`: override inner loop count per histogram sample.
145	  `inner=1` measures single-call latency (each sample = one step).
146	  Higher inner measures back-to-back / burst rate (each sample = N
147	  steps averaged, hides per-call jitter and parking costs).
148	- `--pin CORES`: pin bench threads to logical CPUs. `CORES` is a
149	  comma-separated list with optional ranges: `0,1`, `0-5`, `0,3-5,7`.
150	  Treated as a **core pool** indexed positionally with wrap-around, so
151	  thread `i` gets `pool[i % pool.len()]`. Examples:
152	  - `--pin 0,1` pins a 2-thread bench to logical CPUs 0 and 1.
153	  - `--pin 0,0` co-locates two threads on the same CPU
154	    (oversubscription, which measures contention).
155	  - `--pin 0-11` defines a 12-CPU pool for larger fanout benches;
156	    threads wrap over it.
157	
158	  A `CORES` value that names a `[profiles]` entry in the
159	  [config file](#config-file) expands to that profile's core spec,
160	  `--pin smt` with `smt = "0,12"` configured is exactly `--pin 0,12`.

content.text:
Both answers come from the cell's anatomy:

**`+-x.x%` is the steadiness rating**: the relative standard deviation of the delivered clock across the *settled* stretch (the part the share percentage covers). It answers "once the box settled, how still is still?" — `+-0.0%` is a truly parked clock (your 7600x), and `+-0.3%` is the 3900X's governor micro-wandering inside the 1% stability band that "settled" tolerates. It's the same units as the number before it only by coincidence: the share (`86%`) is *how much of the warm* was settled, the rating (`+-0.3%`) is *how tightly the clock held* during that settled part.

content.text:
All green (fmt, clippy, 121 tests, install), and the evidence rule is live — this batch shows no evidence-free shares at all: verified cells with letters, and run 5's unverifiable/moving case reading `00%` with an F.

On your question — **nothing is failing at the read level, and that's the important distinction.** Every read of `cpuinfo_avg_freq` on this box succeeds. What's unreliable is *attribution*: the sampler reads the clock of whichever core the workload is on at that instant, the unpinned scheduler is free to move the workload between cores, and on a per-core-boost chip like the 3900X different cores genuinely run at different speeds at the same moment. So an unpinned run doesn't *have* a single "the clock" — that's scheduling plus per-core DVFS, not a code defect. Sampling the current core is also the right choice, not a bug: the only clock that explains the timing is the one under the workload. We could read any fixed core's file from anywhere (sysfs allows it), but core 0's clock is meaningless while the work runs on core 17.

Given that, the code now does the three defensible things: it keeps the dominant core's story (the one honest per-core series an unpinned run yields), it refuses to certify "settled" without at least two readings from that core in the settled stretch (one reading has zero range and can attest nothing — this also killed the `18%`-grades-B absurdity you flagged: that run now reads `00% F`), and it reserves the bare no-GHz share exclusively for boxes whose driver exposes no delivered clock, where timing-only is genuinely all there is.

The real cure is the one the harness already carries: **pin the run**. Under `--pin`, workload and sampler sit on one core, every sample is attributable, and the cells read like your 7600x table. An unpinned qualify on a wandering many-core box honestly failing is the tool working — that configuration *isn't* fit for precision A/B. Whether `qualify-environment` should pass `--pin` to its children by default is a real design question for the qualify rung: unpinned measures the box as users run it, pinned measures the box at its best, and maybe it should report both.

The plain version: the clock reads fine — the problem is that an unpinned program wanders between cores that run at different speeds, so no single core's clock describes it. The code now says "settled" only when it has real evidence, says "not settled, F" when it can't verify, and the way to make every run verifiable is to pin the benchmark to one core, which the tool already supports.

The rung still awaits your go for the commit description.

Todo rank 1 added ("Rethink environment rating", with the day's open questions as its seed) and the list renumbered. Here is the description for review:

**Title** (50 chars):

```
fix: the settle cell shows the clock's journey
```

**Body** (75-col wrap):

```
The settle cell printed the measurement floor as a measurement: on a
healthy run the scan succeeded at the first probe and the cell read
`0.01s @4.09GHz`, the time being that probe's timestamp rather than
anything measured, and the state a single number with no story of
how the box got there. Reviewing real runs on two boxes exposed
deeper holes behind the cosmetic one.

* The cell's numbers answered no reader's question: the scan
  timestamp was noise beside the warm budget, and a state without
  its journey cannot separate a box ready all along from one that
  arrived at the last moment.
  - The cell is now the clock's journey: start and settled state
    (`4.84->5.24GHz`), the settled share of the warm as a
    zero-padded percent with `00%` reserved for never-settled, and
    a steadiness rating, the settled stretch's relative stdev. `-v`
    adds a tick-per-step clock profile line.
* An unpinned run's clock series mixes cores at different speeds,
  so its statistics rated scheduler placement rather than the clock
  (+-11.9% mixed against +-0.2% pinned on the same box), and gates
  that bail on missing samples certified claims with no evidence.
  - Every clock statistic reads the dominant CPU only, the scan's
    gate ranges over that core's readable samples, and on a box
    with a readable clock a stretch with fewer than two readings
    does not certify: it reads `00%` with an F rather than an
    unverifiable share.
* The settle verdict had no vote in any grade, and a fast late ramp
  can finish inside the bench's first batches where no timing
  detector sees it, so never-settled runs graded A.
  - The settled share is a graded signal: its letter prints beside
    the cell, folds into the warmup row's worst, and qualify's
    summary counts never-settled runs at 00% instead of skipping
    them.
- `qualify-environment`'s parser and table follow the format, and
  README's settle documentation is rewritten around the cell
  anatomy it had drifted from.
```

Two things to confirm with your push go:

1. **Push target**: the cycle's bookmark is `port-measure-reproducibility`, and every prior rung of this cycle landed with `main` riding along at the same commit. I'll run `vc-x1 push port-measure-reproducibility --title ... --body ...` — tell me if you want `main` advanced with it as before, or left behind this time.
2. I'll re-run full validation immediately before the push, since the Todo edits landed after the last green run.
